title: New York Minute
full_review:
Twin sisters with polar-opposite personalities take a bite out of the Big Apple in the cotton-candy comedy "New York Minute" (Warner Bros.).

Dubbed "the most powerful young women in Hollywood," Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen have literally grown up in the public eye, cutting their teeth, almost literally, on the hit TV series "Full House," where they shared the role of Michelle Tanner, starting when they were 9 months old. They played Michelle until 1995.
So now that they're approaching age 18, what do they do in between running a billion dollar retail-and-entertainment empire? They produce a movie to star in where they each get to play their own part -- with sweet but slight results.

The dimpled duplicates play Jane (Ashley) and Roxy (Mary-Kate) Duncan, mismatched twins who live on Long Island with their somewhat aloof dad, whose medical practice has required him to miss many of the important events in his daughters' lives. Further friction is caused by Jane, a superorganized over-achiever, assuming a maternal mantle since the death of their mother, a move resented by her rebellious slacker sis.

Borrowing a plot device or two from "Ferris Bueller's Day Off," the whole movie takes place in the space of one day. Buttoned-up Jane has to deliver a speech at Columbia University in New York City as part of a prestigious competition with a scholarship to Oxford hanging in the balance.

Meanwhile, the academically challenged Roxy is planning to skip school and try to slip her band's demo tape to recording execs at a music-video shoot in midtown. Begrudgingly, the sparring siblings hop the same Gotham-bound train.

But things change in a New York minute when Jane loses her day planner which has her speech in it. After a series of clumsily contrived mishaps the girls somehow get entangled in a shady, black market DVD piracy scheme operating out of Chinatown.

They are pursued by a faux-Fu Manchu gangster (Andy Richter), who is after a computer chip that his straphanging associate had planted in Jane's bag.

Also hot on their trail is Max Lomax (Eugene Levy), an overzealous truancy officer who sees Roxy as his ticket into the crime-fighting big leagues and who tracks his punk rock prey through the city with Ahab-like tenacity.

Before all is said and done, Jane and Roxy not only work on mending their relationship, but cross romantic paths with a cute bike messenger (Jared Padalecki) and a hunky senator's son (Riley Smith).

While "New York Minute" resembles many of their earlier straight-to-video endeavors, the Olsen twins are surprisingly appealing.

The fact that they are actually sisters helps make both their bonding and bickering more believable and goes a long way to pick up their performances when their acting ability falters.

Those unfamiliar with their off-screen retail juggernaut may be surprised to see how they have blossomed into attractive young women since their "Full House" days.

However, being still on the cusp of adulthood, they retain more than a scent of apple-cheeked innocence -- which they try to erase by shaking their newly bloomed booties in mini-skirts during a frenetic concert scene and traipsing through Time Square in bath towels.

Richter is nothing short of embarrassing and his stereotyping of Asian mannerisms may offend some viewers. Levy steals the show as the bungling bloodhound.

Director Dennie Gordon's decision to shoot on location in Manhattan (with Toronto standing in for some shots) lends the film energy and, if nothing else, a modicum of authenticity. Keen-eyed New Yorkers will have fun picking out the usual logistical inaccuracies.

Overall, the frothy but forgettable movie imparts a positive, family-friendly message. And while no one will mistake its screwball silliness for great -- or even good -- filmmaking, compared to the harder-edged fare being force-fed to young viewers, most parents would take this kind of fresh-scrubbed fluff in a New York minute.

Due to some slight sibling issues and mild sensuality, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
